title: Thessalonica
summary: Thessalonica was a major Roman Macedonian city where Paul, Silas, and Timothy established a community addressed by First and Second Thessalonians and narrated in Acts 17.
historical_context: Located on the Thermaic Gulf and Via Egnatia, Thessalonica was a free city and provincial center with local civic institutions. First-century inscriptions attest politarchs, the title used in Acts 17, while later monuments must be dated separately.
second_temple_context: Paul begins in the synagogue, reasons from the Scriptures, and forms a mixed community within a first-century Jewish and Greco-Roman setting.
canonical_context: Acts 17 narrates the mission and opposition in the city; First and Second Thessalonians address the resulting community's faith, suffering, communal life, and eschatological hope.
literary_context: Acts 17:1-9 compresses the founding conflict into a mission narrative, whereas the Thessalonian letters address the community directly. Narrative and epistolary perspectives should be compared without forcing every detail into one chronology.
covenantal_significance: The Thessalonian mission shows Israel's Scriptures being proclaimed in a Macedonian city and a predominantly Gentile assembly learning to serve the living God and await Jesus.
canonical_role: Thessalonica connects Luke's Macedonian mission narrative with two letters that preserve the community's pastoral, ethical, and eschatological questions.

interpretive_notes.note: The first-century politarch inscription supports the local appropriateness of Acts' title but does not independently verify every event in Acts 17.
Later Roman graves and epitaphs from Thessalonica are local comparisons, not direct evidence of what Paul's audience believed around 50 CE.
